extracted.intended_audience: machine-learning researchers and conference paper authors (NIPS/NeurIPS submitters)
extracted.subtask_description: A first-person report on a NIPS experiment that duplicated paper reviews; discusses review score dimensions, meta-reviews, rebuttal discussion, and how score combinations map to accept/reject outcomes. Useful for authors seeking to understand conference review dynamics and thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality (review score)
rubrics_metrics.description: A numeric 'Quality' score assigned by reviewers (examples in the post: Set 1 = 9, 6, 6; Set 2 = 5, 3, 6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality scores strongly influence acceptance: the author notes that a 9/6/6 quality profile gives a high chance of acceptance, whereas a 5/3/6 profile is a certain non-acceptance. Use aggregate quality scores as a primary signal for accept/reject decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact (review score)
rubrics_metrics.description: A numeric 'Impact' score with textual descriptors given in examples (e.g., 2 labeled 'high', 1 labeled 'incremental').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impact is used to judge novelty or significance; low 'incremental' impact scores (1) can weigh against acceptance even if technical quality is reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence (review score)
rubrics_metrics.description: A numeric 'Confidence' score indicating how certain the reviewer is (examples: 3 = 'fairly confident', 4 = 'confident but not certain', 5 = 'Absolutely certain').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidence reflects the reviewer’s certainty about their assessment; higher confidence strengthens the weight of that reviewer’s quality/impact scores in decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-review content and recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: A meta-review summarizing contribution and making an accept/reject recommendation (example meta-review: 'The paper introduces a new incremental gradient method... has a nice discussion of related methods, and it has a simpler proof that will be of interest to researchers. Recommendation: Accept.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-reviews synthesize reviewer comments and explicitly recommend a disposition. They may highlight novelty, clarity, relation to prior work, and proof simplicity. Meta-reviewers can recommend acceptance even when some numeric scores are low, or conversely justify rejection; their text explains the committee stance and suggested next steps for authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author rebuttal and post-rebuttal reviewer discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Process note: reviewers discussed the paper after the author rebuttal and some reviewers changed or reaffirmed positions (example: 'The reviewers discussed the paper after the author rebuttal, and all reviewers ultimately felt that the paper could use some additional polish before publishing.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rebuttal phase can prompt reviewers to re-evaluate and discuss; it can lead to convergence or further divergence. Authors should use rebuttals to address critiques, but be aware decisions may still be influenced by post-rebuttal discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readiness for publication / polish
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether the manuscript is sufficiently polished for the venue (example: 'The paper we submitted was fairly rough in its initial state, and the reviewers suggested lots of improvements... the paper needed additional polish').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the idea is strong, lacking polish (clarity, presentation, completeness of proofs/experiments) can lead reviewers or meta-reviewers to recommend rejection or request revisions. Authors should address critiques and improve presentation before resubmission to other venues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review consistency / inter-reviewer variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Desideratum for the review process: consistency across independent review panels. The NIPS experiment duplicated 10% of papers and the author's paper received highly discrepant verdicts (one set a clear accept, the other a clear reject).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large discrepancies illustrate randomness/luck in reviewer assignment; consistency is a concern but hard to guarantee. Authors and organizers should be aware that different reviewer sets can produce very different outcomes; tracking and potentially reforming processes (e.g., reviewer calibration, discussion procedures) may help but there is no easy solution.
